title: Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning and Data
text: Computer systems designed to perform tasks that       commonly require human-like capabilities: recognizing patterns, understanding language, classifying information or interpreting images.
An approach within AI in which systems learn patterns from data rather than relying exclusively on explicitly programmed rules.
For many machine-learning applications, examples of data and their correct labels are used to train or          evaluate models. Those labels come from annotation work.
Annotation is not a side activity. For supervised learning the labelled dataset is the teaching material the model learns from, which is why annotation quality sets a ceiling on model quality.
Keep this section short and concrete. Trainees do not need machine-learning theory; they need to understand why their labels matter and what happens downstream if they are wrong.
Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning and Data
notes:
Three definitions, kept deliberately brief. Avoid going deeper into model architectures — it is not needed and it loses non-technical trainees.
Useful framing: the model does not know anything about cars. It only knows what thousands of people told it a car looks like. If those people disagreed, the model learns the disagreement.
Ask for a show of hands: who has used a product that relies on this (voice assistants, photo search, translation)? Connect the abstract to something they use.

title: From Baby to Genius: How AI Learns
text: From Baby to Genius: How AI Learns
notes: Talk track. Top row is Kofi, bottom row is AI; follow the numbers left to right. 1 Born / Collect data: Kofi soaks up sounds, faces and pictures. AI developers gather huge amounts of text, images, video and audio. 2 ABC / Clean data: Kofi learns letters. AI data is cleaned, organised and broken into small pieces called tokens. 3 First words / Tokens: Kofi joins letters into AN and IS. AI turns each token into numbers (embeddings) so it can see how they relate. 4 More words / Build a brain: Kofi links CAT to a real cat. Developers build the neural network, the model's brain. 5 Sentences / Training: Kofi says 'The cat is sleeping'. AI trains like going to the gym, adjusting billions of settings to predict the next word. 6 Corrections / Feedback: teachers correct KAT to CAT. AI errors are measured and fixed; human feedback fine-tunes its answers. 7 Grown up / Ready to help: Kofi holds conversations and solves problems. The AI is deployed: you ask it something and it responds.

title: Our Main Service Areas
text: Three service areas across image, text and audio data. Each uses a different annotation technique, but the same quality discipline applies to all three.

Whatever the data type, the correct output is defined by the approved task specification — not by the technique. The same guideline review, calibration and quality control apply across all three areas.
notes:
Use this to place the trainee's own work within the wider service offering. Most will work in one area; they should know the other two exist.
Image processing is where this programme concentrates, because it is where the demonstration dataset and the SYNAPSE tools sit. The five techniques listed are the ones taught in the annotation week.
If participants ask which area they will be assigned to, that comes from the project, not from the training. Note that text and audio work use different tools and different acceptance criteria.
The callout is the bridge back to the quality module: the technique changes, the discipline does not.

title: Semantic Segmentation
text: Every pixel in the image is given a class label, turning the whole scene into a colour-coded map.
Fill each region with its class colour
Keep borders tight where classes meet
notes: Semantic segmentation labels every pixel. Point out that each colour is a class, not an individual object: all cars share one colour. Emphasise that no pixel may be left unlabelled.

title: Polyline
text: Connected line segments trace thin, continuous structures that have length but no real area.
Place points along the line, end to end
Add more points wherever the line curves
Keep each line one continuous object
Example: both road edges and the centre line traced point by point
notes: Polylines are for things that are long and thin, such as lane markings, kerbs, cables and rivers. The annotator clicks points along the line; more points are needed on curves.

title: Polygon
text: Points placed around an object’s edge form a closed shape that follows its exact outline.
Click vertices along the object’s edge
Add points wherever the outline bends
Close the shape back at the first point
Example: a person, a car and a tree outlined vertex by vertex
notes: Polygons give a much tighter fit than a box, which matters for irregular shapes like people and trees. Compare the tree outline here with the bounding box on the next slide.

title: Bounding Box
text: A rectangle drawn tightly around each object shows where it is and what it is.
Draw one box per object, then label it
Flag objects that are hidden or cut off
Example: three cars, a person and a traffic light, each in its own box
notes: Bounding boxes are the fastest and most common technique. The key quality rule is tightness: the box touches the object’s edges with no gap and nothing cut off. Even small, distant cars get their own box.

title: Key Point
text: Single points mark specific landmarks, such as body joints, so shape and movement can be measured.
Place each point on its exact landmark
Follow the point order in the guideline
Example: 17 body keypoints joined into a skeleton
notes: Key points are about precise position and consistent order: left shoulder is always point 6, for example. When a joint is hidden, annotators still mark it but flag it as occluded, as the guideline specifies.

title: LiDAR and Big Data
text: Two further areas. One is annotation in three dimensions; the other is the data engineering that surrounds every annotation project.
Annotation of three-dimensional point-cloud data, where depth and orientation matter.
Label every point in a scan according to its approved class.
Enclose objects in three dimensions, with position and orientation.
The engineering around the Labeling: where data comes from, how it is prepared, stored, reported and built on.
Database   Structure, store and maintain project datasets.
Data Visualization   Turn production and quality data into readable reporting.
Data Crawling   Collect source data at scale from agreed origins.
Data Preparation   Clean, format and organise raw data before annotation.
Software Development   Build the tooling and integrations the work depends on.

LiDAR is annotation work with its own tools and acceptance criteria. Big Data is what makes any annotation project possible without prepared data and reliable reporting, the Labeling cannot start or be measured.
notes:
Two areas with very different character, which is why they are presented differently.
LiDAR is annotation in three dimensions. It needs suitable data, suitable tools and more practice than the 2D techniques — navigating a point cloud is the hardest part for new annotators, not the Labeling rule.
Big Data is not annotation at all. It is the surrounding engineering: where the data comes from, how it is cleaned and stored, and how production and quality figures are reported back. Annotators rarely see it, but every delay in data preparation shows up later as idle annotation capacity.
If asked how these relate to the training: LiDAR techniques appear in the annotation week as 3D bounding box and 3D semantic segmentation; Big Data does not, and is a separate service line.

title: 3D Segmentation
text: Every point in a LiDAR scan is labelled with its class, so the whole 3D scene is understood.
Label every point with its approved class
Rotate the scan to check from all angles
Keep clean edges where classes touch
notes: A LiDAR scan is a cloud of 3D points measured by laser. 3D segmentation gives every point a class, the 3D version of semantic segmentation. Point out the rings on the ground (each is one laser beam) and the dark gaps behind cars and people, where the laser cannot see.

title: 3D Bounding Box
text: A 3D box (cuboid) encloses each object, recording its position, size and the direction it faces.
Fit length, width and height to the points
Turn the box to face the direction of travel
Keep box sizes steady across frames
Example: points coloured by height; the white line on each box shows which way the object faces
notes: Unlike a 2D box, a cuboid has depth and a heading. The white line on top of each box shows which way the object faces; the oncoming car’s box points the other way. Boxes should hug the points and keep the same size for the same object across frames.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR AN ANNOTATOR
You will rarely be told which product your labels end up in. Treat every task as if the output were going into use tomorrow, because in most of these sectors it is.
notes:
The two original slides have been combined. Splitting ten sectors across two identical layouts made the list look like two different things when it is one.
Do not read the list. Pick three sectors the group will recognise and describe what the annotation work actually looks like in each — the right-hand column gives you the line for every one.
Useful question for the room: which of these sectors would be most affected by a Labeling error, and why? Healthcare, automobile and defense usually come up, which opens the point about critical criteria that cannot be compensated for by a good overall score.
The callout is the behavioural point. Annotators who assume their work is a training exercise treat it differently from those who assume it is going into production.

title: Three Pillars, Four Enablers
text: The strategy rests on three delivery pillars, supported by four cross-cutting enablers that make the pillars usable, safe, funded and fair.
High-performance computing; three             AI-capable data centres in five years.
Stronger cybersecurity, powered by green  energy.
Data governance, secure sharing and         interoperability standards.
High-quality local datasets for training AI models.
Funding for localized models and startup  scaling.
Markets created for Kenyan AI products.
AI foundations in schools, specialised tertiary and industry training,                placements and apprenticeships.
National AI policy, risk and safety standards, regulatory sandboxes, and AI-specific legislation in time.
Grants, funds, public-private         partnerships, special economic     zones.  and investment incentives.
Ethical impact assessments, complaint and redress mechanisms, bias and      representation, public AI literacy.
The pillars build capability. The enablers decide whether that capability is trusted, affordable, staffed and fairly            distributed , which is why all four run across all three.
notes:
The structure is the message: three pillars that build capability, four enablers that determine whether it is usable.
Pillar 2 is the one closest to this audience. 'High-quality local datasets for training AI models' is a policy commitment to exactly the work annotators and QA reviewers do, and it is the line to point at when someone asks whether annotation is a long-term career.
Pillar 1 carries the only hard, dated commitment on the slide: three AI-capable data centres within five years. Expect that to be the number people remember.
Enabler 7 pairs with the training's ethics content: ethical impact assessments in public-sector AI and citizen redress mechanisms are the governance equivalent of the quality-assurance discipline taught here.

notes: On the left is the routine labelers practise every day of the training: read the guideline, label in SYNAPSE, check and fix work after inspection, then report daily output, issues and reflection. On the right, SYNAPSE sits at the centre because once you know it, other tools feel familiar. Image editors and design tools use the same zoom, layers, selection and shape logic as the labeling canvas. ArcGIS works with polygons on map layers, like polygon labeling. Excel, PowerPoint and Word are taught on Day 1 and are used to track and report output. Knowing how labeled data trains AI helps you use Generative AI well. Other labeling platforms such as CVAT or Label Studio run the same tasks with a different interface. Photoshop, GIMP, Figma, Canva, ArcGIS, CVAT and Label Studio are suggested next steps, not part of the training.
